entries.0f064ce6471b51d97b87662027cd0a779762ce4a: <div sID="gen18920" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="26" osisID="Ezek.26" sID="Ezek.26"/> <div eID="gen18920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18921" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18922" type="x-p"/> The prophet had soon done with those four nations that he set his face against in the foregoing chapters; for they were not at that time very considerable in the world, nor would their fall make any great noise among the nations nor any figure in history. But the city of Tyre is next set to the bar; this, being a place of vast trade, was known all the world over; and therefore here are three whole chapters, this and the two that follow, spent in the prediction of the destruction of Tyre. We have "the burden of Tyre," <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18">Isa. xxiii.</reference> It is but just mentioned in Jeremiah, as sharing with the natives in the common calamity, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.22">ch. xxv. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">xxvii. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.47.4">xlvii. 4</reference>. But Ezekiel is ordered to be copious upon that head. In this chapter we have, I. The sin charged upon Tyre, which was triumphing in the destruction of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. The destruction of Tyrus itself foretold. 1. The extremity of this destruction: it shall be utterly ruined, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.4-Ezek.25.6">ver. 4-6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.12-Ezek.25.14">12-14</reference>. 2. The instruments of this destruction, many nations (<reference osisRef="Ezek.25.3">ver. 3</reference>), and the king of Babylon by name with his vast victorious army, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.7-Ezek.25.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. 3. The great surprise that this should give to the neighbouring nations, who would all wonder at the fall of so great a city and be alarmed at it, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.15-Ezek.25.21">ver. 15-21</reference>.
entries.d7cd399d4383eecfe965a6d125cbf3913f458d49: <div eID="gen18922" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18921" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Burden of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And it came to pass in the eleventh year, in the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the month, <hi type="italic">that</hi> the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came unto me, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Son of man, because that Tyrus hath said against Jerusalem, Aha, she is broken <hi type="italic">that was</hi> the gates of the people: she is turned unto me: I shall be replenished, <hi type="italic">now</hi> she is laid waste: <hi type="super">3</hi> Therefore thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> against thee, O Tyrus, and will cause many nations to come up against thee, as the sea causeth his waves to come up. <hi type="super">4</hi> And they shall destroy the walls of Tyrus, and break down her towers: I will also scrape her dust from her, and make her like the top of a rock. <hi type="super">5</hi> It shall be <hi type="italic">a place for</hi> the spreading of nets in the midst of the sea: for I have spoken <hi type="italic">it,</hi> saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> : and it shall become a spoil to the nations. <hi type="super">6</hi> And her daughters which <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the field shall be slain by the sword; and they shall know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">7</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; Behold, I will bring upon Tyrus Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, a king of kings, from the north, with horses, and with chariots, and with horsemen, and companies, and much people. <hi type="super">8</hi> He shall slay with the sword thy daughters in the field: and he shall make a fort against thee, and cast a mount against thee, and lift up the buckler against thee. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers. <hi type="super">10</hi> By reason of the abundance of his horses their dust shall cover thee: thy walls shall shake at the noise of the horsemen, and of the wheels, and of the chariots, when he shall enter into thy gates, as men enter into a city wherein is made a breach. <hi type="super">11</hi> With the hoofs of his horses shall he tread down all thy streets: he shall slay thy people by the sword, and thy strong garrisons shall go down to the ground. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they shall make a spoil of thy riches, and make a prey of thy merchandise: and they shall break down thy walls, and destroy thy pleasant houses: and they shall lay thy stones and thy timber and thy dust in the midst of the water. <hi type="super">13</hi> And I will cause the noise of thy songs to cease; and the sound of thy harps shall be no more heard. <hi type="super">14</hi> And I will make thee like the top of a rock: thou shalt be <hi type="italic">a place</hi> to spread nets upon; thou shalt be built no more: for I the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> have spoken <hi type="italic">it,</hi> saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18924" type="x-p"/> This prophecy is dated in the eleventh year, which was the year that Jerusalem was taken, and <hi type="italic">in the first day of the month,</hi> but it is not said what month, some think the month in which Jerusalem was taken, which was the fourth month, others the month after; or perhaps it was the first month, and so it was the first day of the year. Observe here, <div eID="gen18924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18925" type="x-p"/> I. The pleasure with which the Tyrians looked upon the ruins of Jerusalem. Ezekiel was a great way off, in Babylon, but God told him what Tyrus said against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Aha! she is broken,</hi> broken to pieces, that was <hi type="italic">the gates of the people,</hi> to whom there was a great resort and where there was a general rendezvous of all nations, some upon one account and some upon another, and I shall get by it; all the wealth, power, and interest, which Jerusalem had, it is hoped, shall be turned to Tyre, and so <hi type="italic">now</hi> that <hi type="italic">she is laid waste I shall be replenished.</hi>" We do not find that the Tyrians had such a hatred and enmity to Jerusalem and the sanctuary as the Ammonites and Edomites had, or were so spiteful and mischievous to the Jews. They were men of business, and of large acquaintance and free conversation, and therefore were not so bigoted, and of such a persecuting spirit, as the narrow souls that lived retired and knew not the world. All their care was to get estates, and enlarge their trade, and they looked upon Jerusalem not as an enemy, but as a rival. Hiram, king of Tyre, was a good friend to David and Solomon, and we do not read of any quarrels the Jews had with the Tyrians; but Tyre promised herself that the fall of Jerusalem would be an advantage to her in respect of trade a commerce, that now she shall have Jerusalem's customers, and the great men from all parts that used to come to Jerusalem for the accomplishing of themselves, and to spend their estates there, will now come to Tyre and spend them there; and whereas many, since the Chaldean army became so formidable in those parts, had retired into Jerusalem, and brought their estates thither for safety, as the Rechabites did, now they will come to Tyre, which, being in a manner surrounded with the sea, will be thought a place of greater strength than Jerusalem, and thus the prosperity of Tyre will rise out of the ruins of Jerusalem. Note, To be secretly pleased with the death or decay of others, when we are likely to get by it, with their fall when we may thrive upon it, is a sin that does most easily beset us, but is not thought to be such a bad thing, and so provoking to God, as really it is. We are apt to say, when those who stand in our light, in our way, are removed, when they break or fall into disgrace, "We shall be <hi type="italic">replenished</hi> now that they are <hi type="italic">laid waste.</hi>" But this comes from a selfish covetous principle, and a desire to be <hi type="italic">placed alone in the midst of the earth,</hi> as if we grudged that any should live by us. This comes from a want of that love to our neighbour as to ourselves which the law of God so expressly requires, and from that inordinate love of the world as our happiness which the love of God so expressly forbids. And it is just with God to blast the designs and projects of those who thus contrive to raise themselves upon the ruins of others; and we see they are often disappointed. <div eID="gen18925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18926" type="x-p"/> II. The displeasure of God against them for it. The providence of God had done well for Tyrus. Tyrus was a pleasant and wealthy city, and might have continued so if she had, as she ought to have done, sympathized with Jerusalem in her calamities and sent her an address of condolence; but when, instead of that, she showed herself pleased with her neighbour's fall, and perhaps sent an address of congratulation to the conquerors, then God says, <hi type="italic">Behold, I am against thee, O Tyrus!</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.3">v. 3</reference>. And let her not expect to prosper long if God be against her. <div eID="gen18926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18927" type="x-p"/> 1. God will bring formidable enemies upon her: <hi type="italic">Many nations shall come against thee,</hi> an army made up of many nations, or one nation that shall be as strong as many. Those that have God against them may expect all the creatures against them; for what peace can those have with whom God is at war? They shall come pouring in as <hi type="italic">the waves of the sea,</hi> one upon the neck of another, with an irresistible force. The person is named that shall bring this army upon them—<hi type="italic">Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, a king of kings,</hi> that had many kings tributaries to him and dependents on him, besides those that were his captives, <reference osisRef="Dan.2.37-Dan.2.38">Dan. ii. 37, 38</reference>. He is that <hi type="italic">head of gold.</hi> He shall come with a vast army, <hi type="italic">horses and chariots,</hi> &c., all land-forces. We do not find that he had any naval force, or any thing wherewith he might attack it by sea, which made the attempt the more difficult, as we find <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18">ch. xxix. 18</reference>, where it is called a <hi type="italic">great service which he served against Tyrus.</hi> He shall besiege it in form (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">make a fort, and cast a mount,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.9">v. 9</reference>) shall <hi type="italic">set engines of war against the walls.</hi> His troops shall be so numerous as to raise a dust that shall cover the city, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.10">v. 10</reference>. They shall make a noise that shall even <hi type="italic">shake the walls;</hi> and they shall shout at every attack, as soldiers do when they <hi type="italic">enter a city</hi> that is <hi type="italic">broken up;</hi> the horses shall prance with so much fury and violence that they shall even <hi type="italic">tread down the streets</hi> though so ever well paved. <div eID="gen18927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18928" type="x-p"/> 2. They shall do terrible execution. (1.) The enemy shall make themselves masters of all their fortifications, shall <hi type="italic">destroy the walls</hi> and <hi type="italic">break down the towers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4">v. 4</reference>. For what walls are so strongly built as to be a fence against the judgments of God? Her <hi type="italic">strong garrisons shall go down to the ground,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.11">v. 11</reference>. And the walls shall be broken down, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.12">v. 12</reference>. The city held out a long siege, but it was taken at last. (2.) A great deal of blood shall be shed: <hi type="italic">Her daughters who are in the field,</hi> the cities upon the continent, which were subject to Tyre as the mother-city, the inhabitants of them <hi type="italic">shall be slain by the sword,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.6">v. 6</reference>. The invaders begin with those that come first in their way. And (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.11">v. 11</reference>) <hi type="italic">he shall slay thy people with the sword;</hi> not only the soldiers that are found in arms, but the burghers, shall be <hi type="italic">put to the sword,</hi> the king of Babylon being highly incensed against them for holding out so long. (3.) The wealth of the city shall all become a spoil to the conqueror (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.12">v. 12</reference>): They <hi type="italic">shall make a prey of the merchandise.</hi> It was in hope of the plunder that the city was set upon with so much vigour. See the vanity of riches, that they are <hi type="italic">kept for the owners to their hurt;</hi> they entice and recompense thieves, and not only cease to benefit those who took pains for them and were duly entitled to them, but are made to serve their enemies, who are thereby put into a capacity of doing them so much the more mischief. (4.) The city itself shall be laid in ruins. All the <hi type="italic">pleasant houses</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">destroyed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.12">v. 12</reference>), such as were pleasantly situated, beautified, and furnished, shall become a heap of rubbish. Let none please themselves too much in their pleasant houses, for they know not how soon they may see the desolation of them. Tyre shall be utterly ruined; the enemy shall not only pull down the houses, but shall carry away <hi type="italic">the stones and the timber,</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">lay them in the midst of the water,</hi> not to be recovered, or ever made use of again. Nay (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4">v. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will scrape her dust from her;</hi> not only shall the loose dust be blown away, but the very ground it stands upon shall be torn up by the enraged enemy, carried off, and laid <hi type="italic">in the midst of the water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.12">v. 12</reference>. The <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> is <hi type="italic">in the dust;</hi> that dust shall be all taken away, and then the city must fall of course. When Jerusalem was destroyed it was <hi type="italic">ploughed like a field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.3.12">Mic. iii. 12</reference>. But the destruction of Tyre is carried further than that; the very soil of it shall be scraped away, and it shall be made <hi type="italic">like the top of a rock</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4">v. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.14">14</reference>), pure rock that has no earth to cover it; it shall only be a place <hi type="italic">for the spreading of nets</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">v. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.14">14</reference>); it shall serve fishermen to dry their nets upon and mend them. (5.) There shall be a full period to all its mirth and joy (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will cause the noise of thy songs to cease.</hi> Tyre had been a joyous city (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.7">Isa. xxiii. 7</reference>); with her songs she had courted customers to deal with her in a way of trade. But now farewell all her profitable commerce and pleasant conversation; Tyre is no more a place either of business or of sport. <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> It shall be <hi type="italic">built no more</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.14">v. 14</reference>), not built any more as it had been, with such state and magnificence, nor built any more in the same place, within the sea, nor built any where for a long time; the present inhabitants shall be destroyed or dispersed, so that this Tyre shall be <hi type="italic">no more.</hi> For <hi type="italic">God has spoken it</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">v. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.14">14</reference>); and when what he has said is accomplished <hi type="italic">they shall know</hi> thereby that <hi type="italic">he is the Lord,</hi> and <hi type="italic">not a man that he should lie nor the son of man that he should repent.</hi>
entries.6ebe04a2fd09853a1b99e2e225f214c31bda34dc: <div eID="gen18928" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Burden of Tyre. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 588.)</title> <div sID="gen18929" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> Thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> to Tyrus; Shall not the isles shake at the sound of thy fall, when the wounded cry, when the slaughter is made in the midst of thee? <hi type="super">16</hi> Then all the princes of the sea shall come down from their thrones, and lay away their robes, and put off their broidered garments: they shall clothe themselves with trembling; they shall sit upon the ground, and shall tremble at <hi type="italic">every</hi> moment, and be astonished at thee. <hi type="super">17</hi> And they shall take up a lamentation for thee, and say to thee, How art thou destroyed, <hi type="italic">that wast</hi> inhabited of seafaring men, the renowned city, which wast strong in the sea, she and her inhabitants, which cause their terror <hi type="italic">to be</hi> on all that haunt it! <hi type="super">18</hi> Now shall the isles tremble in the day of thy fall; yea, the isles that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the sea shall be troubled at thy departure. <hi type="super">19</hi> For thus saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ; When I shall make thee a desolate city, like the cities that are not inhabited; when I shall bring up the deep upon thee, and great waters shall cover thee; <hi type="super">20</hi> When I shall bring thee down with them that descend into the pit, with the people of old time, and shall set thee in the low parts of the earth, in places desolate of old, with them that go down to the pit, that thou be not inhabited; and I shall set glory in the land of the living; <hi type="super">21</hi> I will make thee a terror, and thou <hi type="italic">shalt be</hi> no <hi type="italic">more:</hi> though thou be sought for, yet shalt thou never be found again, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <div eID="gen18929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18930" type="x-p"/> The utter ruin of Tyre is here represented in very strong and lively figures, which are exceedingly affecting. <div eID="gen18930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18931" type="x-p"/> 1. See how high, how great, Tyre had been, how little likely ever to come to this. The remembrance of men's former grandeur and plenty is a great aggravation of their present disgrace and poverty. Tyre was <hi type="italic">a renowned city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.17">v. 17</reference>), famous among the nations, the <hi type="italic">crowning</hi> city (so she is called <reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">Isa. xxiii. 8</reference>), a city that had crowns in her gift, honoured all she smiled upon, crowned herself and all about her. She was <hi type="italic">inhabited of seas,</hi> that is, of those that trade at sea, of those who from all parts came thither by sea, bringing with them the <hi type="italic">abundance of the seas</hi> and <hi type="italic">the treasures hidden in the sand.</hi> She was <hi type="italic">strong in the sea,</hi> easy of access to her friends, but to her enemies inaccessible, fortified by a <hi type="italic">wall of water,</hi> which made her impregnable. So that <hi type="italic">she</hi> with her pomp, <hi type="italic">and her inhabitants</hi> with their pride, <hi type="italic">caused their terror to be on all that haunted</hi> that city, and upon any account frequented it. It was well fortified, and formidable in the eyes of all that acquainted themselves with it. Every body stood in awe of the Tyrians and was afraid of disobliging them. Note, Those who know their strength are too apt to cause terror, to pride themselves in frightening those they are an over-match for. <div eID="gen18931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18932" type="x-p"/> 2. See how low, how little, Tyre is made, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.19-Ezek.26.20">v. 19, 20</reference>. This <hi type="italic">renowned city</hi> is made a <hi type="italic">desolate city,</hi> is no more frequented as it has been; there is no more resort of merchants to it; it is <hi type="italic">like the cities not inhabited,</hi> which are no cities, and having none to keep them in repair, will go to decay of themselves. Tyre shall be like a city overflowed by an inundation of waters, which <hi type="italic">cover</hi> it, and upon which the <hi type="italic">deep</hi> is <hi type="italic">brought up.</hi> As the waves had formerly been its defence, so now they shall be its destruction. She shall be <hi type="italic">brought down with those that descend into the pit,</hi> with the cities of the old world that were under water, and with <hi type="italic">Sodom and Gomorrah,</hi> that lie in the bottom of the Dead Sea. Or, she shall be in the condition of those who have been long buried, of the <hi type="italic">people of old time,</hi> who are old inhabitants of the silent grace, who are quite rotted away under ground and quite forgotten above ground; such shall <hi type="italic">Tyre be, free among the dead, set in the lower parts of the earth,</hi> humbled, mortified, reduced. It shall be <hi type="italic">like the places desolate of old,</hi> as well as like persons dead of old; it shall be like other cities that have formerly been in like manner deserted and destroyed. It shall <hi type="italic">not be inhabited</hi> again; none shall have the courage to attempt the rebuilding of it upon that spot, so that <hi type="italic">it shall be no more;</hi> The Tyrians shall be lost among the nations, so that people will look in vain for Tyre in Tyre: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt be sought for, and never found again.</hi> New persons may build a new city upon a new spot of ground hard by, which they may call <hi type="italic">Tyre,</hi> but Tyre, as it is, shall never be any more. Note, The strongest cities in this world, the best-fortified and best-furnished, are subject to decay, and may in a little time be brought to nothing. In the history of our own island many cities are spoken of as in being when the Romans were here which now our antiquaries scarcely know where to look for, and of which there remains no more evidence than Roman urns and coins digged up there sometimes accidentally. But in the other world we look for a city that shall stand for ever and flourish in perfection through all the ages of eternity. <div eID="gen18932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18933" type="x-p"/> 3. See what a distress the inhabitants of Tyre are in (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">There is a great slaughter made in the midst of thee,</hi> many slain, and great men. It is probable that, when the city was taken, the generality of the inhabitants were put to the sword. Then did <hi type="italic">the wounded cry,</hi> and they cried in vain, to the pitiless conquerors; they cried <hi type="italic">quarter,</hi> but it would not be given them; the wounded are <hi type="italic">slain</hi> without mercy, or, rather, that is the only mercy that is shown them, that the second blow shall rid them out of their pain. <div eID="gen18933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18934" type="x-p"/> 4. See what a consternation all the neighbours are in upon the fall of Tyre. This is elegantly expressed here, to show how astonishing it should be. (1.) the <hi type="italic">islands</hi> shall <hi type="italic">shake at the sound of thy fall</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.15">v. 15</reference>), as, when a great merchant breaks, all that he deals with are shocked by it, and begin to look about them; perhaps they had effects in his hands, which they are afraid they shall lose. Or, when they see one fail and become bankrupt of a sudden, in debt a great deal more than he is worth, it makes them afraid for themselves, lest they should do so too. Thus <hi type="italic">the isles,</hi> which thought themselves safe in the embraces of the sea, when they see Tyrus fall, shall <hi type="italic">tremble</hi> and <hi type="italic">be troubled,</hi> saying, "What will become of us?" And it is well if they make this good use of it, to take warning by it not to be secure, but to stand in awe of God and his judgments. The sudden fall of a great tower shakes the ground round about it; thus all the islands in the Mediterranean Sea shall feel themselves sensibly touched by the destruction of Tyre, it being a place they had so much knowledge of, such interests in, and such a constant correspondence with. (2.) The <hi type="italic">princes of the sea</hi> shall be affected with it, who ruled in those islands. Or the rich merchants, who live like princes (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">Isa. xxiii. 8</reference>), and the masters of ships, who command like princes, these shall condole the fall of Tyre in a most compassionate and pathetic manner (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall come down from their thrones,</hi> as neglecting the business of their thrones and despising the pomp of them. They shall <hi type="italic">lay away their robes</hi> of state, <hi type="italic">their broidered garments,</hi> and shall <hi type="italic">clothe themselves</hi> all over with <hi type="italic">tremblings,</hi> with sackcloth that will make them shiver. Or they shall by their own act and deed make themselves to tremble upon this occasion; they shall <hi type="italic">sit upon the ground</hi> in shame and sorrow; they shall <hi type="italic">tremble every moment</hi> at the thought of what has happened to Tyre, and for fear of what may happen to themselves; for what island is safe if Tyre be not? They shall <hi type="italic">take up a lamentation for thee,</hi> shall have elegies and mournful poems penned upon the fall of Tyre, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.17">v. 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">How art thou destroyed!</hi> [1.] It shall be a great surprise to them, and they shall be affected with wonder, that a place so well fortified by nature and art, so famed for politics and so full of money, which is the sinews of war, that held out so long and with so much bravery, should be taken at last (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.21">v. 21</reference>): <hi type="italic">I make thee a terror.</hi> Note, It is just with God to make those a terror to their neighbours, by the suddenness and strangeness of their punishment, who make themselves a terror to their neighbours by the abuse of their power. Tyre had <hi type="italic">caused her terror</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.17">v. 17</reference>) and now is made a terrible example. [2.] It shall be a great affliction to them, and they shall be affected with sorrow (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.17">v. 17</reference>); they shall <hi type="italic">take up a lamentation for Tyre,</hi> as thinking it a thousand pities that such a rich and splendid city should be thus laid in ruins. When Jerusalem, the holy city, was destroyed, there were no such lamentations for it; it was <hi type="italic">nothing</hi> to <hi type="italic">those that passed by</hi> (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.12">Lam. i. 12</reference>); but when Tyre, the trading city, fell, it was universally bemoaned. Note, Those who have the world in their hearts lament the loss of great men more than the loss of good men. [3.] It shall be a loud alarm to them: <hi type="italic">They shall tremble in the day of thy fall,</hi> because they shall have reason to think that their own turn will be next. If Tyre fall, who can stand? <hi type="italic">Howl, fir-trees, if such a cedar be shaken.</hi> Note, The fall of others should awaken us out of our security. The death or decay of others in the world is a check to us, when we dream that our mountain <hi type="italic">stands strongly and shall not be moved.</hi> <div eID="gen18934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18935" type="x-p"/> 5. See how the irreparable ruin of Tyre is aggravated by the prospect of the restoration of Israel. Thus shall Tyre sink <hi type="italic">when I shall set glory in the land of the living,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">v. 20</reference>. Note, (1.) The holy land is the <hi type="italic">land of the living;</hi> for none but holy souls are properly living souls. Where living sacrifices are offered to the living God, and where the lively oracles are, there <hi type="italic">the land of the living</hi> is; there David hoped to <hi type="italic">see the goodness of the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Ps. xxvii. 13</reference>. That was a type of heaven, which is indeed the <hi type="italic">land of the living.</hi> (2.) Though this land of the living may for a time lie under disgrace, yet God will again <hi type="italic">set glory</hi> in it; the glory that had departed shall return, and the restoration of what they had been deprived of shall be so much more their glory. God will himself be the glory of the lands that are the lands of the living. (3.) It will aggravate the misery of those that have their portion in the land of the dying, of those that are for ever dying, to behold the happiness of those, at the same time, that shall have their everlasting portion in the land of the living. When the rich man was himself in torment he saw Lazarus in the bosom of Abraham, and glory set for him in the land of the living.  <chapter eID="Ezek.26"/> <div eID="gen18935" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b83f9ea7cf065d7cba3bb4ac18d9edaba064ae5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11499"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 26</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ezek.26.1-Ezek.26.21">Eze 26:1-21</reference>. The Judgment on Tyre through Nebuchadnezzar (TWENTY-SIXTH THROUGH Twenty-eighth Chapters).</title> <div sID="gen20808" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">In the twenty-sixth chapter, Ezekiel sets forth:--</hi>(1) Tyre's sin; (2) its doom; (3) the instruments executing it; (4) the effects produced on other nations by her downfall. In the twenty-seventh chapter, a lamentation over the fall of such earthly splendor. In the twenty-eighth chapter, an elegy addressed to the king, on the humiliation of his sacrilegious pride. Ezekiel, in his prophecies as to the heathen, exhibits the dark side only; because he views them simply in their hostility to the people of God, who shall outlive them all. Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18">Is 23:1-18</reference>), on the other hand, at the close of judgments, holds out the prospect of blessing, when Tyre should turn to the Lord.<div eID="gen20808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11499"/>1. The specification of the date, which had been omitted in the case of the four preceding objects of judgment, marks the greater weight attached to the fall of Tyre.<div eID="gen20809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20810" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eleventh year--</hi>namely, after the carrying away of Jehoiachin, the year of the fall of Jerusalem. The number of the month is, however, omitted, and the day only given. As the month of the taking of Jerusalem was regarded as one of particular note, namely, the fourth month, also the fifth, on which it was actually destroyed (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">Jr 52:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.12.13">12, 13</reference>), Rabbi David reasonably supposes that Tyre uttered her taunt at the close of the fourth month, as her nearness to Jerusalem enabled her to hear of its fall very soon, and that Ezekiel met it with his threat against herself on "the first day" of the fifth month. <div eID="gen20810" type="x-p"/>
entries.599eb1c823aa4e9586ef39e056cd2b2df670693a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11500"/><div sID="gen20811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11500"/><hi type="bold">2. Tyre--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Josh.19.29">Jos 19:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.7">2Sa 24:7</reference>), literally, meaning "the rock-city," Zor; a name applying to the island Tyre, called New Tyre, rather than Old Tyre on the mainland. They were half a mile apart. "New Tyre," a century and a half before the fall of Jerusalem, had successfully resisted Shalmaneser of Assyria, for five years besieging it (Menander, from the Tyrian archives, quoted by Josephus, Antiquities, 9.14. 2). It was the stronger and more important of the two cities, and is the one chiefly, though not exclusively, here meant. Tyre was originally a colony of Zidon. Nebuchadnezzar's siege of it lasted thirteen years (<reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18">Eze 29:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18">Is 23:1-18</reference>). Though no profane author mentions his having succeeded in the siege, Jerome states he read the fact in Assyrian histories.<div eID="gen20811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Aha!--</hi>exultation over a fallen rival (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.21">Psa 35:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen20812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20813" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she ... that was the gates--</hi>that is, the single gate composed of two folding doors. Hence the verb is singular. "Gates" were the place of resort for traffic and public business: so here it expresses a mart of commerce frequented by merchants. Tyre regards Jerusalem not as an open enemy, for her territory being the narrow, long strip of land north of Philistia, between Mount Lebanon and the sea, her interest was to cultivate friendly relations with the Jews, on whom she was dependent for corn (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Eze 27:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.9">1Ki 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.12.20">Ac 12:20</reference>). But Jerusalem had intercepted some of the inland traffic which she wished to monopolize to herself; so, in her intensely selfish worldly-mindedness, she exulted heartlessly over the fall of Jerusalem as her own gain. Hence she incurred the wrath of God as pre-eminently the world's representative in its ambition, selfishness, and pride, in defiance of the will of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.9">Is 23:9</reference>).<div eID="gen20813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">she is turned unto me--</hi>that is, the mart of corn, wine, oil, balsam, &c., which she once was, is transferred to me. The caravans from Palmyra, Petra, and the East will no longer be intercepted by the market ("the gates") of Jerusalem, but will come to me. <div eID="gen20814" type="x-p"/>
entries.a116e2babc61a24155da3059f88f04834be2362f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11501"/><div sID="gen20815" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11501"/><hi type="bold">3-4. nations ... as the sea ... waves--</hi>In striking contrast to the boasting of Tyre, God threatens to bring against her Babylon's army levied from "many nations," even as the Mediterranean waves that dashed against her rock-founded city on all sides.<div eID="gen20815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">scrape her dust ... make her ... top of ... rock--</hi>or, "a bare rock" [Grotius]. The soil which the Tyrians had brought together upon the rock on which they built their city, I will scrape so clean away as to leave no dust, but only the bare rock as it was. An awful contrast to her expectation of filling herself with all the wealth of the East now that Jerusalem has fallen. <div eID="gen20816" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7c157e8218bc11cba8d4ecd147ac526878439a5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11502"/><div sID="gen20817" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11502"/><hi type="bold">5. in the midst of the sea--</hi>plainly referring to New Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.27.32">Eze 27:32</reference>). <div eID="gen20817" type="x-p"/>
entries.28e3424e26f5317a260305ffae7e55a5b2dcf2ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11503"/><div sID="gen20818" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11503"/><hi type="bold">6. her daughters ... in the field--</hi>The surrounding villages, dependent on her in the open country, shall share the fate of the mother city. <div eID="gen20818" type="x-p"/>
entries.d16d5099d296e04ed57e8b97eb8f9178a775f493: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11504"/><div sID="gen20819" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11504"/><hi type="bold">7. from the north--</hi>the original locality of the Chaldeans; also, the direction by which they entered Palestine, taking the route of Riblah and Hamath on the Orontes, in preference to that across the desert between Babylon and Judea.<div eID="gen20819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20820" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">king of kings--</hi>so called because of the many kings who owned allegiance to him (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.28">2Ki 18:28</reference>). God had delegated to him the universal earth-empire which is His (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.47">Da 2:47</reference>). The Son of God alone has the right and title inherently, and shall assume it when the world kings shall have been fully proved as abusers of the trust (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.15">1Ti 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.12-Rev.14.19">Re 17:12-14; 19</reference>:15, 16). Ezekiel's prophecy was not based on conjecture from the past, for Shalmaneser, with all the might of the Assyrian empire, had failed in his siege of Tyre. Yet Nebuchadnezzar was to succeed. Josephus tells us that Nebuchadnezzar began the siege in the seventh year of Ithobal's reign, king of Tyre. <div eID="gen20820" type="x-p"/>
entries.e94eed3a4eee8f7e54e0522c8d7e4a07187cb993: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11505"/><div sID="gen20821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11505"/><hi type="bold">9. engines of war--</hi>literally, "an apparatus for striking." "He shall apply the stroke of the battering-ram against thy walls." Havernick translates, "His enginery of destruction"; literally, the "destruction (not merely the stroke) of his enginery."<div eID="gen20821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">axes--</hi>literally, "swords." <div eID="gen20822" type="x-p"/>
entries.be37ec8e9a004b2568419c76dd110604c6e4c320: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11506"/><div sID="gen20823" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11506"/><hi type="bold">10. dust--</hi>So thick shall be the "dust" stirred up by the immense numbers of "horses," that it shall "cover" the whole city as a cloud.<div eID="gen20823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20824" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">horses ... chariots--</hi>As in <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.3-Ezek.26.5">Eze 26:3-5</reference>, New Tyre on the insular rock in the sea (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.23.2">Is 23:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">4, 6</reference>) is referred to; so here, in <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.9-Ezek.26.11">Eze 26:9-11</reference>, Old Tyre on the mainland. Both are included in the prophecies under one name.<div eID="gen20824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20825" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wheels--</hi>Fairbairn thinks that here, and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.24">Eze 23:24</reference>, as "the wheels" are distinct from the "chariots," some wheelwork for riding on, or for the operations of the siege, are meant. <div eID="gen20825" type="x-p"/>
entries.e87412d7e03c4a4490eb6f680ccd1e320d15156b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11507"/><div sID="gen20826" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11507"/><hi type="bold">11. thy strong garrisons--</hi>literally, "the statutes of thy strength"; so the forts which are "monuments of thy strength." Maurer understands, in stricter agreement with the literal meaning, "the statues" or "obelisks erected in honor of the idols, the tutelary gods of Tyre," as Melecarte, answering to the Grecian Hercules, whose temple stood in Old Tyre (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.43.13">Jr 43:13</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen20826" type="x-p"/>
entries.e747696cdc9e34c3e011da35b524c0f756cbbd44: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11508"/><div sID="gen20827" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11508"/><hi type="bold">12. lay thy stones ... timber ... in ... midst of ... water--</hi>referring to the insular New Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.3">Eze 26:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.4">Eze 27:4</reference>, 25, 26). When its lofty buildings and towers fall, surrounded as it was with the sea which entered its double harbor and washed its ramparts, the "stones ... timbers ... and dust" appropriately are described as thrown down "in the midst of the water." Though Ezekiel attributes the capture of Tyre to Nebuchadnezzar (see on <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.18">Eze 29:18</reference>), yet it does not follow that the final destruction of it described is attributed by him to the same monarch. The overthrow of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar was the first link in the long chain of evil--the first deadly blow which prepared for, and was the earnest of, the final doom. The change in this verse from the individual conqueror "he," to the general "they," marks that what he did was not the whole, but only paved the way for others to complete the work begun by him. It was to be a progressive work until she was utterly destroyed. Thus the words here answer exactly to what Alexander did. With the "stones, timber," and rubbish of Old Tyre, he built a causeway in seven months to New Tyre on the island and so took it [Curtius, 4, 2], 322 B.C. <div eID="gen20827" type="x-p"/>
entries.7a34172697230aca3c5fad14ef07ed7a2e35f9eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11509"/><div sID="gen20828" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11509"/>13. Instead of the joyousness of thy prosperity, a death-like silence shall reign (<reference osisRef="Isa.24.8">Is 24:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.34">Jr 7:34</reference>). <div eID="gen20828" type="x-p"/>
entries.6656a1bd7036a670186ca72039c331900b95fc61: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11510"/><div sID="gen20829" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11510"/>14. He concludes in nearly the same words as he began (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.4">Eze 26:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">5</reference>).<div eID="gen20829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20830" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">built no more--</hi>fulfilled as to the mainland Tyre, under Nebuchadnezzar. The insular Tyre recovered partly, after seventy years (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.17">Is 23:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.23.18">18</reference>), but again suffered under Alexander, then under Antigonus, then under the Saracens at the beginning of the fourteenth century. Now its harbors are choked with sand, precluding all hope of future restoration, "not one entire house is left, and only a few fishermen take shelter in the vaults" [Maundrell]. So accurately has God's word come to pass. <div eID="gen20830" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d57dcd68ba19e356d5c2098725d469f596a19a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11511"/><div sID="gen20831" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11511"/>15-21. The impression which the overthrow of Tyre produced on other maritime nations and upon her own colonies, for example, Utica, Carthage, and Tartessus or Tarshish in Spain.<div eID="gen20831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20832" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">isles--</hi>maritime lands. Even mighty Carthage used to send a yearly offering to the temple of Hercules at Tyre: and the mother city gave high priests to her colonies. Hence the consternation at her fall felt in the widely scattered dependencies with which she was so closely connected by the ties of religion, as well as commercial intercourse.<div eID="gen20832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20833" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shake--</hi>metaphorically: "be agitated" (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.21">Jr 49:21</reference>). <div eID="gen20833" type="x-p"/>

entries.d6eacb76d83fd3ab5e9554c043e4ba350ab20789: <div eID="gen31965" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31966" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31967" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31967" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31966" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31968" type="x-p"/> This prophecy, beginning here and ending in the twentieth verse of the twenty-eighth chapter, is a declaration of the judgments of God against Tyre, a very famous commercial city of antiquity, which was taken by Nebuchadnezzar after an arduous siege of thirteen years. The prophet begins with introducing Tyre insulting Jerusalem, and congratulating herself on the prospect of accession to her commerce now that this city was no more, <reference osisRef="Eze.26.1">Eze 26:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eze.26.2">Eze 26:2</reference>. Upon which God denounces utter destruction to Tyre, and the cities depending on her, <reference osisRef="Eze.26.3-Eze.26.6">Eze 26:3-6</reference>. We have then a particular account of the person raised up in the course of the Divine providence to accomplish this work. We see, as it were, his mighty hosts, (which are likened to the waves of the sea for their multitude), raising the mounds, setting the engines, and shaking the walls; we hear the noise of the horsemen, and the sound of their cars; we see the clouds of smoke and dust; we see the sword bathed in blood, and hear the groans of the dying. Tyre, (whose buildings were very splendid and magnificent, and whose walls were one hundred and fifty feet in height, with a proportionable breadth), immediately disappears; her strong (and as she thought impregnable) towers are thrown down; and her very dust is buried in the sea. Nothing remains but the bare rock, <reference osisRef="Eze.26.7-Eze.26.14">Eze 26:7-14</reference>. The scene is then varied. The isles and adjacent regions, by a very strong and beautiful figure, are represented to be shaken, as with a mighty earthquake by violent concussion occasioned by the fall of Tyre. The groans of the dying reach the ears of the people inhabiting these regions. Their princes, alarmed for themselves and grieved for Tyre, descend from their thrones, lay aside their robes, and clothe themselves with - sackcloth? - no, but with trembling! Arrayed in this astonishing attire, the prophet introduces them as a chorus of mourners, lamenting Tyre in a funeral song or dirge, as customary on the death of renowned personages. And pursuing the same image still farther, in the person of God, he performs the last sad office for her. She is brought forth from her place in solemn pomp; the pit is dug for her; and she is buried, to rise no more, <reference osisRef="Eze.26.15-Eze.26.21">Eze 26:15-21</reference>. Such is the prophecy concerning Tyre, comprehending both the city on the continent and that on the island, and most punctually fulfilled in regard to both. That on the continent was razed to the ground by Nebuchadnezzar, b.c. 572, and that on the island by Alexander the Great, b.c. 332. And at present, and for ages past, this ancient and renowned city, once the emporium of the world, and by her great naval superiority the center of a powerful monarchy, is literally what the prophet has repeatedly foretold it should be, and what in his time was, humanly speaking, so highly improbable - a Bare rock, a place to spread nets on! <div eID="gen31968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31969" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31970" type="x-p"/> The eleventh year - This was the year in which Jerusalem was taken; the eleventh of the captivity of Jeconiah, and the eleventh of the reign of Zedekiah. What month we are not told, though the day is mentioned. There have been many conjectures about this, which are not of sufficient consequence to be detailed.
entries.34baa326753763e9cf120b8f82cde91be2277714: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen31970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31971" type="x-p"/> Tyrus hath said - From this it would appear that Jerusalem had been taken, which was on the fourth month of this year; but it is possible that the prophet speaks of the event beforehand. <div eID="gen31971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31972" type="x-p"/> She is broken that was the gates of the people - Jerusalem, a general emporium. <div eID="gen31972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31973" type="x-p"/> I shall be replenished - The merchandise that went to Jerusalem will come to me, (to Tyre.).
entries.ce8cad9821f604fae19126eff839bfd04a8daad9: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen31973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31974" type="x-p"/> Will cause many nations to come up against thee - We have already seen that the empire of the Chaldeans was composed of many different provinces, and that Nebuchadnezzar's army was composed of soldiers from different nations: these may be the people meant; but I doubt whether this may not refer to the different nations which in successive ages fought against Tyre. It was at last finally destroyed in the sixteenth century of the Christian era.
entries.5e281776fbbe4019db5271885e5e71e253273905: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen31974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31975" type="x-p"/> I will also scrape her dust from her - I will totally destroy her fortifications, and leave her nothing but a barren rock, as she was before. This cannot refer to the capture of Tyre by Nebuchadnezzar. It flourished long after his time.
entries.adc1cc391668c70a1cc464c8ba21286c475ce19f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31976" type="x-p"/> A place for the spreading of nets - A place for the habitation of some poor fishermen, who spent the fishing season there, and were accustomed to dry their nets upon the rocks. See on <reference osisRef="Eze.26.11">Eze 26:11</reference> (note).
entries.3ed181205972a44c2376809bdb332003673df82f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31977" type="x-p"/> And her daughters - The places dependent on Tyre. As there were two places called Tyre, one on the main land, and the other on a rock in the sea, opposite to that on the main land, sometimes the one seems to be spoken of, and sometimes the other. That on the land, Palaetyre, was soon taken; but that in the sea cost Nebuchadnezzar thirteen years of siege and blockade. The two formed only one city, and one state.
entries.9bef3c42c9da7270d34467bcba098fcedfc03e2c: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen31977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31978" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadrezzar - king of kings - An ancient title among those proud Asiatic despots shahinshah and padshah, titles still in use.
entries.527fffcd3e282c3e1f93cc8fd3a14ce353f0034a: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen31978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31979" type="x-p"/> Thy daughters in the field - This seems to be spoken of Palaetyre, or Tyre on the main land; for forts, mounts, engines of war, horses, and chariots could not be brought to act against the other.
entries.af5011384e4561bfa6ff7839b597bceaadb4ecb2: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen31979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31980" type="x-p"/> And they shall lay thy stones and thy timber and thy dust in the midst of the water - This answers to the taking of Tyre by Alexander; he actually took the timbers, stones, rubbish, etc. of old Tyre, and filled up the space between it and new Tyre, and thus connected the latter with the main land; and this he was obliged to do before he could take it.
entries.a13fce75506f33a188bcfb5d9d47c4c13b7d2bb3: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen31980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31981" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt be built no more - If this refer to Nebuchadnezzar's capture of the city, old Tyre must be intended: that was destroyed by him, and never rebuilt. But I doubt whether the whole of this prophecy do not refer to the taking of Tyre by Alexander, three hundred years after its capture by Nebuchadnezzar. Indeed it may include more recent conquests of this important city. It went through a variety of vicissitudes till 1289, when it and the neighboring towns were sacked and ravaged by the Mamelukes. Mr. Maundrell, who visited this place, says, "it is a Babel of broken walls, pillars, vaults, etc., there being not so much as one entire house left! Its present inhabitants are only a few poor wretches, harbouring themselves in the vaults, and subsisting chiefly on fishing; who seem to be preserved in this place by Divine Providence as a visible argument how God has fulfilled his word concerning Tyre, that it should be the top of a rock, a place for fishers to dry their nets on."
entries.edfe72baecff5beaa80d74b819eb349e925f2f4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen31981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31982" type="x-p"/> The isles shake at the sound of thy fall - All those which had traded with this city, which was the grand mart, and on which they all depended. Her ruin involved them all, and caused general wailing.
entries.3460bf6a61846691f7eb81a882451307e627c1ac: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen31982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31983" type="x-p"/> The princes of the sea - The chief maritime states, such as Leptis, Utica, Carthage, Gades, etc. See Calmet.
entries.f102b14004f0f19e68aab5af8706526dd4a07ec8: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen31983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31984" type="x-p"/> Wast strong in the sea - The strength of Tyre was so great, that Alexander despaired of being able to reduce it unless he could fill up that arm of the sea that ran between it and the main land. And this work cost his army seven months of labor.
entries.8e2c711c9ab13d7a237e545f1177fa4f31a7d7b1: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen31984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31985" type="x-p"/> And I shall set glory in the land of the living - Judea so called, the land of the living God.
entries.17c1cb7a7a800ee9f37057602145f56e89f5c99b: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen31985" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31986" type="x-p"/> Yet shalt thou never be found again - This is literally true; there is not the smallest vestige of the ancient Tyre, that which was erected on the main land. Even the ground seems to have been washed away; and the new Tyre is in nearly a similar state. I think this prophecy must be extended to the whole duration of Tyre. If it now be found to be in the state here described, it is sufficient to show the truth of the prophecy. And now it is found precisely in the state which the above prophetic declarations, taken according to the letter, point out! No word of God can ever fall to the ground. <div eID="gen31986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31987" type="x-p"/> Notwithstanding the former destructions, Tyre was a place of some consequence in the time of St. Paul. There was a Church there, (see <reference osisRef="Act.21.3">Act 21:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Act.21.4">Act 21:4</reference>, etc.), which afterwards became famous. Calmet observes, it afforded a great number of martyrs for the Christian Church.  <chapter eID="Ezek.26"/> <div eID="gen31987" type="x-p"/>

entries.723c51b7d29c5cc51547e3ab32056748f9c105e1: <div eID="gen15029" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Against Tyre and Sidon - Ezekiel 26-28</title> <div sID="gen15030" type="x-p"/> The greater portion of these three chapters is occupied with the prophecy concerning Tyre, which extends from <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.1">Eze 26:1</reference> to Eze 28:19. The prophecy against Sidon is limited to <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.20">Eze 28:20</reference>-26. The reason for this is, that the grandeur and importance of Phoenicia were concentrated at that time in the power and rule of Tyre, to which Sidon had been obliged to relinquish the hegemony, which it had formerly possessed over Phoenicia. The prophecy against Tyre consists of four words of God, of which the first (Ezekiel 26) contains the threat of destruction to the city and state of Tyre; the second (Ezekiel 27), a lamentation over this destruction; the third (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.1-Ezek.28.10">Eze 28:1-10</reference>), the threat against the king of Tyre; the fourth (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.11-Ezek.28.19">Eze 28:11-19</reference>), a lamentation over his fall. <div eID="gen15030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15031" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.1">Eze 26:1</reference> <div eID="gen15031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15032" type="x-p"/> In four sections, commencing with the formula, “thus saith the Lord,” Tyre, the mistress of the sea, is threatened with destruction. In the first strophe (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.2-Ezek.26.6">Eze 26:2-6</reference>) there is a general threat of its destruction by a host of nations. In the second (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.7-Ezek.26.14">Eze 26:7-14</reference>), the enemy is mentioned by name, and designated as a powerful one; and the conquest and destruction emanating from his are circumstantially described. In the third (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.15-Ezek.26.18">Eze 26:15-18</reference>), the impression which this event would produce upon the inhabitants of the islands and coast-lands is depicted. And in the fourth (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.19-Ezek.26.21">Eze 26:19-21</reference>), the threat is repeated in an energetic manner, and the prophecy is thereby rounded off. <div eID="gen15032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15033" type="x-p"/> This word of God bears in the introduction to the date of its delivery to the prophet and enunciation by him. - Eze 26:1. <hi type="italic">It came to pass in the eleventh year, on the first of the month, that the word of Jehovah came to me, saying.</hi> - The eleventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin was the year of the conquest and destruction of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">Jer 52:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jer 52:12</reference>), the occurrence of which is presupposed in <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.2">Eze 26:2</reference> also. There is something striking in the omission of the number of the month both here and in <reference osisRef="Ezek.32.17">Eze 32:17</reference>, as the day of the month is given. The attempt to discover in the words בּאחד an indication of the number of the month, by understanding לחדשׁ as signifying the first month of the year: “on the first as regards the month,” equivalent to, “in the first month, on the first day of it” (lxx, Luther, Kliefoth, and others), is as forced and untenable as the notion that that particular month is intended which had peculiar significance for Ezekiel, namely, the month in which Jerusalem was conquered and destroyed. The first explanation is proved to be erroneous by <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.2">Eze 26:2</reference>, where the destruction of Jerusalem, which occurred in the fifth month of the year named, is assumed to have already happened. The second view is open to the objection that the conquest of Jerusalem happened in the fourth month, and the destruction in the fifth (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.6">Jer 52:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Jer.52.12">Jer 52:12</reference>); and it cannot be affirmed that the conquest was of less importance to Ezekiel than the destruction. We cannot escape the conclusion, therefore, that the number of the month has been dropped through a corruption of the text, which has occurred in copying; but in that case we must give up all hope of being able to determine what the month really was. The conjecture offered by Ewald and Hitzig, that one of the last months of the year is intended, because Ezekiel could not have known before then what impression the conquest of Jerusalem had made upon Tyre, stands or falls with the naturalistic view entertained by these writers with regard to prophecy.
entries.61daa19416265701592e55ec07a07411436e89aa: <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.2-Ezek.26.14">Eze 26:2-14</reference> <div eID="gen15033" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Tyre shall be broken and utterly destroyed</title> <div sID="gen15034" type="x-p"/> Eze 26:2.<hi type="italic">Son of man, because Tyre saith concerning Jerusalem, “Aha, the door of the nations is broken; it turneth to me; I shall become full; she is laid waste;”</hi> Eze 26:3. <hi type="italic">Therefore thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Behold, I will come upon thee, O Tyre, and will bring up against thee many nations, as the sea bringing up its waves.</hi> Eze 26:4. <hi type="italic">They will destroy the walls of Tyre, and throw down her towers; and I will sweep away her dust from her, and make her a bare rock.</hi> Eze 26:5. <hi type="italic">She shall become a place for the spreading of nets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken it, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah; and she shall become booty for the nations.</hi> Eze 26:6. <hi type="italic">And her daughters which are in the land shall be slain with the sword; and they shall learn that I am Jehovah.</hi> - Tyre, as in the prophecy of Isaiah (Ezekiel 23), is not the city of that name upon the mainland, ἡ πάλαι Τύρος or Παλαίτυρος, Old Tyre, which was taken by Shalmaneser and destroyed by Alexander (as Perizon., Marsh, Vitringa, J. D. Michaelis, and Eichhorn supposed), but Insular Tyre, which was three-quarters of a mile farther north, and only 1200 paces from the land, being built upon a small island, and separated from the mainland by a strait of no great depth (vid., Movers, <hi type="italic">Phoenizier</hi>, II p. 288ff.). This Insular Tyre had successfully resisted the Assyrians (Josephus, <hi type="italic">Antt</hi>. ix. 14. 2), and was at that time the market of the nations; and in Ezekiel’s day it had reached the summit of its greatness as mistress of the sea and the centre of the commerce of the world. That it is against this Tyre that our prophecy is chiefly directed, is evident from <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">Eze 26:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.14">Eze 26:14</reference>, according to which Tyre is to become a bare rock in the midst of the sea, and from the allusion to the daughter cities, בּשּׂדה, in the field, i.e., on the mainland (in <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.6">Eze 26:6</reference>), as contrasted with the position occupied by Tyre upon a rocky island in the sea; and, lastly, from the description given in Ezekiel 27 of the maritime trade of Tyre with all nations, to which Old Tyre never attained, inasmuch as it possessed no harbour (vid., Movers, <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi> p. 176). This may easily be reconciled with such passages as <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.6">Eze 26:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.8">Eze 26:8</reference>, and Ezekiel 27, 28, in which reference is also made to the continental Tyre, and the conquest of Tyre is depicted as the conquest of a land-city (see the exposition of these verses). - The threat against Tyre commences, as in the case of the nations threatened in Ezekiel 25, with a brief description of its sin. Tyre gave expression to its joy at the fall of Jerusalem, because it hoped to derive profit therefrom through the extension of its commerce and increase of its wealth. Different explanations have been given of the meaning of the words put into the mouth of Tyre. “The door of the nations is broken in pieces.” The plural דּלתות indicates the folding doors which formed the gate, and are mentioned in its stead. Jerusalem is the door of the nations, and is so called according to the current opinion of expositors, because it was the centre of the commerce of the nations, i.e., as a place of trade. But nothing is known to warrant the idea that Jerusalem was ever able to enter into rivalry with Tyre as a commercial city. The importance of Jerusalem with regard to other nations was to be found, not in its commerce, nor in the favourable situation which it occupied for trade, in support of which Hävernick refers to Herodotus, iii. 5, and Hitzig to <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.40-Ezek.23.41">Eze 23:40-41</reference>, but in its sanctuary, or the sacred calling which it had received for the whole world of nations. Kliefoth has therefore decided in favour of the following view: That Jerusalem is called a gate of the nations, not because it had hitherto been open to the nations for free and manifold intercourse, but for the very opposite reason, namely, because the gate of Jerusalem had hitherto been closed and barred against the nations, but was now broken in pieces through the destruction of the city, and thereby opened to the nations. Consequently the nations, and notably Tyre, would be able to enter now; and from this fact the Tyrians hoped to derive advantage, so far as their commercial interests were concerned. But this view is not in harmony with the text. Although a gate is opened by being broken in pieces, and one may force an entrance into a house by breaking the door (<reference osisRef="Gen.19.9">Gen 19:9</reference>), yet the expression “door of the nations” cannot signify a door which bars all entrance on the part of the nations, inasmuch as doors and gates are not made to secure houses and cities against the forcible entrance of men and nations, but to render it possible for them to go out and in. Moreover, the supposition that “door of the nations” is equivalent to shutting against the nations, is not in harmony with the words נסבּא אלי which follow. The expression “it has turned to me,” or it is turned to me, has no meaning unless it signifies that through the breaking of the door the stream of the nations would turn away from Jerusalem to Tyre, and therefore that hitherto the nations had turned to Jerusalem. נסבּה  is the 3rd pers. perf. <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi> of סבב, for נסבּה , formed after the analogy of נמס, etc. The missing subject to נסבּה  is to be found <hi type="italic">ad sensum</hi> in דּלתות העמּים. It is not the door itself, but the entrance and streaming in of the nations, which had previously been directed towards Jerusalem, and would now turn to Tyre. There is no necessity, therefore, for Hitzig’s conjecture, that  אמּלאה should be altered into מלאהּ, and the latter taken as the subject. <div eID="gen15034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15035" type="x-p"/> Consequently we must understand the words of the Tyrians as signifying that they had regarded the drawing of the nations to Jerusalem, i.e., the force of attraction which Jerusalem had hitherto exerted upon the nations, as the seat of the divine revelation of mercy, or of the law and judgment of the Lord, as interfering with their endeavour to draw all nations to themselves and gain them over to their purposes, and that they rejoiced at the destruction of Jerusalem, because they hoped that henceforth they would be able to attract the nations to themselves and enrich themselves with their possessions. This does not require that we should accredit the Tyrians with any such insight into the spiritual calling of Jerusalem as would lie beyond their heathen point of view. The simple circumstance, that the position occupied by Jerusalem in relation to the world apparently interfered with the mercantile interests of the Tyrians, would be quite sufficient to excite a malignant pleasure at the fall of the city of God, as the worship of God and the worship of Mammon are irreconcilably opposed. The source from which the envy and the enmity manifesting itself in this malicious pleasure took their rise, is indicated in the last words: “I shall fill myself, she (Jerusalem) is laid waste,” which Jerome has correctly linked together thus: <hi type="italic">quia illa deserta est, idcirco ego implebor</hi>. המּלא, to be filled with merchandise and wealth, as in Eze 27:25. On account of this disposition toward the kingdom of God, which led Tyre to expect an increase of power and wealth from its destruction, the Lord God would smite it with ruin and annihilation. הנני עליך, behold, I will come upon thee, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.8">Eze 13:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.31">Jer 50:31</reference>; Nah 3:5. God will lead a powerful army against Tyre, which shall destroy its walls and towers. Instead of the army, “many nations” are mentioned, because Tyre is hoping to attract more nations to itself in consequence of the destruction of Jerusalem. This hope is to be fulfilled, though in a different sense from that which Tyre intended. The comparison of the advancing army to the advancing waves of the sea is very significant when the situation of Tyre is considered. היּם is the subject to כּהעלות, and the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> is construed with  ל instead of the accusative (compare Ewald, §292 <hi type="italic">c</hi> with §277 <hi type="italic">e</hi>). According to Arrian, ii. 18. 3, and Curtius, iv. 2. 9, 12, and 3. 13, Insular Tyre was fortified all round with lofty walls and towers, which were certainly in existence as early as Nebuchadnezzar’s time. Even the dust of the demolished buildings (עפרהּ) God would sweep away (סחיתי, ἁπ. λεγ., with a play upon שׁחתוּ), so that the city, i.e., the site on which it had stood, would become a bare and barren rock (צחיח סלע, as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.7">Eze 24:7</reference>), a place where fishermen would spread out their nets to dry. “Her daughters” also, that is to say, the towns dependent upon Tyre, “on the field,” i.e., the open country - in other words, their inhabitants - would be slain with the sword. <div eID="gen15035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15036" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.7-Ezek.26.14">Eze 26:7-14</reference> the threat is carried still further. - Eze 26:7. <hi type="italic">For thus saith the Lord Jehovah, Behold, I will bring against Tyre Nebuchadnezzar, the king of Babylon, from the north, the king of kings, with horses, and chariots, and horsemen, and a multitude of much people.</hi> Eze 26:8. <hi type="italic">Thy daughters in the field he will slay with the sword, and he will erect siege-towers against thee, and throw up a rampart against thee, and set up shields against thee,</hi> Eze 26:9. <hi type="italic">And direct his battering-rams against thy walls, and throw down thy towers with his swords.</hi> Eze 26:10. <hi type="italic">From the multitude of his horses their dust will cover thee; from the noise of the horsemen, wheels, and chariots, thy walls will shake when he shall enter into thy gates, as they enter a city broken open.</hi> Eze 26:11. <hi type="italic">With the hoofs of his horses he will tread down all thy streets; thy people he will slay with the sword, and thy glorious pillars will fall to the ground. Eze 26:12. They will make booty of thy possessions, and plunder thy merchandise, destroy thy walls, and throw down thy splendid mansions, and sink thy stones, thy wood, and thy dust in the water.</hi> Eze 26:13. <hi type="italic">I will put an end to the sound of thy songs, and the music of thy harps shall be heard no more.</hi> Eze 26:14. <hi type="italic">I will make thee a bare rock; thou shalt be a place for the spreading of nets, and be built no more; for I Jehovah have spoken it, is the saying of the Lord Jehovah.</hi> - Nebuchadnezzar, the great king of Babylon, - this is the meaning of the rhetorical description in these verses, - will come with a powerful army (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.7">Eze 26:7</reference>), smite with the sword the inland cities dependent upon Tyre. (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.8">Eze 26:8</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.6">Eze 26:6</reference>), then commence the siege of Tyre, destroy its walls and towers (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.26.8">Eze 26:8</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.9">Eze 26:9</reference>), enter with his army the city in which breaches have been made, put the inhabitants to death (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.10">Eze 26:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.11">Eze 26:11</reference>), plunder the treasures, destroy walls and buildings, and cast the ruins into the sea (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.12">Eze 26:12</reference>). <hi type="italic">Nebuchadrezzar</hi>, or <hi type="italic">Nebuchadnezzar</hi> (for the name see the comm. on 2Ki 24:10, is called king of kings, as the supreme ruler of the Babylonian empire, because the kings of conquered provinces and lands were subject to him as vassals (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Isa.10.8">Isa 10:8</reference>). <div eID="gen15036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15037" type="x-p"/> His army consists of war-chariots, and cavalry, and a great multitude of infantry. קהל  are co-ordinate, so far as the rhetorical style is concerned; but in reality עם־רב is subordinate to קהל , as in <reference osisRef="Ezek.23.24">Eze 23:24</reference>, inasmuch as the קהל consisted of עם־רב. On the siege-works mentioned in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ezek.26.8">Eze 26:8</reference></hi>, see the comm. on Eze 4:2. הקים צנּה signifies the construction of a roof with shields, by which the besiegers were accustomed to defend themselves from the missiles of the defenders of the city wall while pursing their labours. Herodotus repeatedly mentions such shield-roofs as used by the Persians (ix. 61. 99, 102), though, according to Layard, they are not to be found upon the Assyrian monuments (see the comm. on <reference osisRef="Nah.2.6">Nah 2:6</reference>). There is no doubt that מחי קב signifies the battering-ram, called כּר in <reference osisRef="Ezek.21.27">Eze 21:27</reference>, though the meaning of the words is disputed. מחי , literally, thrusting or smiting. קבלו, from קבל, to be pointed either קבלּו  or קבלּו  (the form קבלּו  adopted by v. d. Hooght and J. H. Michaelis is opposed to the grammatical rules), has been explained by Gesenius and others as signifying <hi type="italic">res opposita</hi>, that which is opposite; hence מחי קבלו, the thrusting or demolishing of that which stands opposite. In the opinion of others, קבל  is an instrument employed in besieging; but there is nothing in the usage of the language to sustain either this explanation or that adopted by Hävernick, “destruction of his defence.” הרבותיו, his swords, used figuratively for his weapons or instruments of war, “his irons,” as Ewald has very aptly rendered it. The description in <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.10">Eze 26:10</reference> is hyperbolical. The number of horses is so great, that on their entering the city they cover it with dust, and the walls shake with the noise of the horsemen and chariots. 'כּמבואי עיר מב, literally, as the marchings into a broken city, i.e., a city taken by storm, generally are. The simile may be explained from the peculiar situation of Insular Tyre. It means that the enemy will enter it as they march into a land-fortress into which a breach has been made by force. The words presuppose that the besieger has made a road to the city by throwing up an embankment or dam. מצּבות עזּך, the memorial pillars of thy might, and the pillars dedicated to Baal, two of which are mentioned by Herodotus (ii. 44) as standing in the temple of Hercules at Tyre, one of gold, the other of emerald; not images of gods, but pillars, as symbols of Baal. These sink or fall to the ground before the overwhelming might of the foe (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.46.1">Isa 46:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.9">Isa 21:9</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.5.3">1Sa 5:3</reference>). After the slaughter of the inhabitants and the fall of the gods, the plundering of the treasures begins, and then follows the destruction of the city. בּתּי המדּה are not pleasure-houses (“pleasure-towers, or garden-houses of the wealthy merchants,” as Ewald supposes), for there was not space enough upon the island for gardens (Strabo, xvi. 2. 23), but the lofty, magnificent houses of the city, the palaces mentioned in Isa 23:13. Yea, the whole city shall be destroyed, and that so completely that they will sweep stones, wood, and rubbish into the sea. - Thus will the Lord put an end to the exultation and rejoicing in Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.13">Eze 26:13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Isa 14:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Amos.5.23">Amo 5:23</reference>). - The picture of the destruction of this powerful city closes with the repetition of the thought from <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.5">Eze 26:5</reference>, that Tyre shall be turned into a bare rock, and shall never be built again.
entries.6d535aeab9dc25288716d751501933f1c9ab7e1c: <reference osisRef="Ezek.26.15-Ezek.26.18">Eze 26:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen15037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15038" type="x-p"/> The tidings of the destruction of Tyre will produce great commotion in all her colonies and the islands connected with her. - Eze 26:15. <hi type="italic">Thus saith the Lord Jehovah to Tyre, Will not the islands tremble at the noise of thy fall, at the groaning of the wounded, at the slaughter in the midst of thee?</hi> Eze 26:16. <hi type="italic">And all the princes of the sea will come down from their thrones, and will lay aside their robes and take off their embroidered clothes, and dress themselves in terrors, sit upon the earth, and they will tremble every moment, and be astonished at thee.</hi> Eze 26:17. <hi type="italic">They will raise a lamentation for thee, and say to thee: How hast thou perished, thou who wast inhabited from out of the sea, thou renowned city, she who was mighty upon the sea, she and her inhabitants, who inspired all her inhabitants with fear of her!</hi> Eze 26:18. <hi type="italic">Now do the islands tremble on the day of thy fall, and the islands in the sea are confounded at thy departure.</hi> - הלא, <hi type="italic">nonne</hi>, has the force of a direct affirmation. קול מפּלה, the noise of the fall, stands for the tidings of the noise, since the noise itself could not be heard upon the islands. The fall takes place, as is added for the purpose of depicting the terrible nature of the event, at or amidst the groaning of the wounded, and the slaughter in the midst of thee. בּהרג is the infinitive <hi type="italic">Niphal</hi>, with the accent drawn back on account of the following <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>, and should be pointed בּהרג . The word איּים, islands, is frequently used so as to embrace the coast lands of the Mediterranean Sea; we have therefore to understand it here as applied to the Phoenician colonies on the islands and coasts of that sea. The “princes of the sea” are not kings of the islands, but, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.23.8">Isa 23:8</reference>, the merchants presiding over the colonies of Tyre, who resembled princes. כּסאות, not royal thrones, but chairs, as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.4.13">1Sa 4:13</reference>, etc. The picture of their mourning recalls the description in <reference osisRef="Jonah.3.6">Jon 3:6</reference>; it is not derived from that passage, however, but is an independent description of the mourning customs which commonly prevailed among princes.
